extraction.paper_title: HotSpot Thermal Floorplan Solver Using Conjugate Gradient to Speed Up

scenario.figure_or_table: Table 1 (also Tables 2-3, MCNC benchmark, ami49 case)
scenario.description: Solver run-time comparison inside the HotSpot simulated-annealing thermal floorplanner. An LU decomposition solver is compared with a conjugate gradient (CG) solver, with and without Jacobi or SSOR preconditioning, on MCNC benchmarks (xerox, hp, ami33, ami49). The paper reports the ami49 case with 49 blocks as the headline result: 1534.41 s for LU versus 134.7 s for SSOR-CG, about an 11.39x speedup. The paper publishes no block coordinates or dimensions and no per-block powers. Block powers were randomly generated by a Perl script with power density between 1e5 and 1e7 W/m2, and the individual values are not published. It reports no temperature observable; the observables are solver CPU run time and speedup ratio.
scenario.architecture: MCNC benchmark block-level floorplans (ami49 with 49 blocks); a 2D HotSpot block thermal resistance model with no stacked-die, interposer or package details published
scenario.workload: Randomly generated block power trace (Perl random function), power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2 per block; no real workload
scenario.operating_point: Static temperature evaluation within each simulated-annealing iteration; no published ambient temperature, cooling condition or per-block power values

original_setup.solver: HotSpot thermal-resistance block model (R*T=P), with the default LU decomposition solver compared against a conjugate gradient (CG) solver. CG was run unpreconditioned, with a Jacobi preconditioner, and with an SSOR preconditioner. The incremental CG variant reuses the previous SA iteration's solution as the initial estimate (PDF pages 3-5).
original_setup.optimizer: Simulated Annealing thermal floorplanner in HotSpot (hot floorplan). Cost is lambdaA*Area + lambdaT*Temperature + lambdaW*WireLength (PDF pages 3, 5, 6).
original_setup.controller: None. There is no dynamic thermal management or runtime controller. The solver is switched by a command-line parameter, and the model gives a static temperature evaluation inside each SA iteration (PDF pages 2, 5).
original_setup.benchmark: MCNC benchmark circuits xerox (10 blocks), hp (11), ami33 (33) and ami49 (49), plus GSRC n100, n200 and n300 (Table 4). Selected scenario: MCNC ami49 with 49 blocks, LU 1534.41 s versus SSOR-CG 134.7 s, ratio 11.39 (Tables 1-3, PDF pages 6-7). Block powers were randomly generated by a Perl script with power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2 per block, and the individual values are not published. Machine: Ubuntu, Intel Core i5-2300 2.80 GHz, 12 GB memory.

thermal_observable.location: No temperature observable is reported. The paper reports solver CPU run time (s), average per-solve time (s) and speedup ratio. For the selected ami49 scenario the SSOR-CG run time is 134.7 s, the LU run time is 1534.41 s and the ratio is 11.39. The SA cost uses the maximum block temperature, but no value is published.
thermal_observable.aggregation: Not applicable for temperature. Run time is total SA floorplanner CPU time, and the per-solve average is total run time over the number of solver calls.

physical_mismatches.reason: The paper is a numerical linear-solver speed benchmark and reports no temperature, no per-block dimensions or coordinates, no per-block power values, and no ambient or boundary conditions. No complete thermal experiment can be reconstructed from it, so the selected scenario is not steady_2d_relevant.

The optimizer is simulated-annealing floorplanning with a changing placement and a relative-sparse-matrix incremental solver. A fixed-placement thermal evaluation would not reproduce this optimizer or solver behavior.

The model is a 2D HotSpot block thermal resistance model. There is no 3D stacking, interposer or chiplet structure, and no cooling or package specification is published. It is not comparable to chiplet or 2.5D setups.
Block powers come from a random Perl script (power density 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2), so there is no real workload and no transient power trace. There is no controller or reliability analysis.

studio_assumptions: No paper-derived floorplan, power rows or thermal observable exist, so the Studio floorplan is empty.

Any Studio run would be a separate illustrative construction using bundled package and material assumptions. Its generated coordinates and powers would be kept distinct from paper facts, and its temperatures would not be compared numerically to the paper, which reports none.
The Studio solver is not the paper's HotSpot LU or CG solver and runs no simulated-annealing optimizer, so no replication of the paper's run-time results is claimed.

methods.note: The LU vs CG (none/Jacobi/SSOR) solver comparison, the SA cost lambdaA*A+lambdaT*T+lambdaW*W, warm-starting from the previous solution, and the R*T=P model are supported by text on PDF pages 3-6. Two extraction claims are not: the 2D label and the 'static' evaluation. The paper also says HotSpot computes 'dynamic block or grid temperature' (p3), and it never calls the model 2D. The paper's own Algorithm 1 is internally defective (see findings).

code.note: No source code, repository, supplementary link, or HotSpot patch is given in the PDF. The packet assets list is empty. Algorithm 1 and 2 pseudocode is garbled and unusable as an implementation: 'b ? A ? x', 'while (rnorm < precision)', Iter never incremented, and bnorm unused.

parameters.note: The only parameters are the 1e5-1e7 W/m2 density range and the machine spec. The exponents appear as '105' and '107' in the pdftotext output and were interpreted as 10^5 and 10^7 without visual confirmation. No lambda weights, SA schedule (Rcool, Kmoves, Nmax, Rreject), CG tolerance 'precision', SSOR relaxation factor, or random seed are given. Per-block power and temperature are unpublished.

config.note: No HotSpot configuration, ambient temperature, package, heat sink, or boundary conditions are published. The scenario is not a thermal-field reproduction and has no steady/2D thermal setup. kind=custom_2d_steady with an empty floorplan is a placeholder, not a paper-derived configuration.

data.note: The table numbers for ami49 (Table 1 p6: 49 blocks, 1534.41 s, 135801 solves, 1.13E-02; Table 3 p7: 134.7 s, 11.39, 9.92E-04) match the supplied pdftotext text and are arithmetically consistent. They come from a text layer only; no page image was supplied, so the tables and Figures 1-2 were not visually verified. No block coordinates, dimensions, per-block powers, or temperature are available, so no floorplan block has same-scenario power and the paper's observable is solver run time, not a thermal quantity.

findings.reason: The extraction labels the model 'a 2D HotSpot block thermal resistance model' and the evaluation 'static'. The paper never states 2D. Page 3 says HotSpot 'compute[s] the dynamic block or grid temperature' while elsewhere saying 'static temperature computer'. These labels are inferred and mixed in the source.

findings.reason: The text says CG without preconditioner is slower than LU on two small cases. In Table 1 only hp is slower (8.88 vs 7.53). xerox is faster (5.32 vs 5.69, ratio 1.07). The text also says SSOR is 'less better' than Jacobi, although Table 3 shows SSOR is faster. The paper's narrative is unreliable against its own tables.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable, and Studio did not run (simulation status: skipped). The deterministic gate failed because the custom 2D steady experiment has an empty floorplan and no power_w object, while a custom experiment needs 1-128 blocks and powers. Both input_gate_pass and scientific_gate_pass are false, independently_verified is false, simulation_allowed is false and comparison_valid is false. The paper (W2796297998) is a numerical linear-solver benchmark of LU versus conjugate gradient (CG) solvers inside the HotSpot simulated-annealing floorplanner. Its reported observables are solver CPU run time and speedup, not temperature. For the selected MCNC ami49 case (49 blocks) it reports LU at 1534.41 s versus SSOR-CG at 134.7 s, a ratio of about 11.39. No block coordinates, dimensions, per-block powers, ambient or boundary conditions are published, only a random power density range of 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2. No linked assets or repositories were found, so no source commit or placement assumption applies, and no illustrative input.flp or input.ptrace was generated. This is a custom steady 2D scenario, so there is no transient trace. It is not a bundled EV6/GCC adaptation and not a pinned Ascend910 or ATPlace case. No numerical temperature comparison is possible because the paper reports no temperature and no matching location, aggregation, regime or boundary assumptions exist. Any Studio result would not test the paper's run-time claims, since Studio uses a different solver and has no simulated-annealing optimizer or incremental sparse solver. The final verdict is therefore not_2d_applicable with no replication claim. The paper's run-time numbers are reported only as paper-stated values.
limitations: Studio did not run; there is no simulated temperature, floorplan or power output to assess.
The paper reports no temperature observable, so no numerical comparison is valid. Run time and speedup are solver performance metrics, not thermal observables.

The paper publishes no ami49 block coordinates, widths or heights, no per-block powers (only the random density range 1e5 to 1e7 W/m2), and no ambient, package or cooling boundary conditions. The Perl script and random seed are also missing.
The original setup is a simulated-annealing floorplanner with changing placement and an incremental CG solver, which a fixed-placement steady 2D evaluation cannot reproduce.
The model is a 2D HotSpot block resistance model, not a 3D, interposer or chiplet configuration, and it has no transient workload or controller.
No linked assets, repository, source commit or pinned configuration exist, so no source commit or generated placement assumption can be reported.

Evidence quality gaps remain: several evidence items lack valid page or asset locators, the thermal observable lacks a page, unit, location and aggregation, no steady/transient regime is cited, and adversarial code, parameter, config and data checks and independent page review are unresolved.
The gate sets comparison_valid to false; the paper's run-time figures (1534.41 s, 134.7 s, 11.39x) are reported only as paper-stated values and are not replicated or verified.
The mismatches in physical location, aggregation, regime and boundary assumptions are essential, so only qualitative discussion is justified.
